What Is Roofing Marketing? (And Why Most Roofers Get It Wrong)

Roofing marketing is the systematic process of attracting, converting, and retaining homeowners and commercial property managers who need roofing services. It is not door-knocking after a hailstorm. It is not buying shared leads from HomeAdvisor and hoping for the best. And it is definitely not posting random photos on Facebook once a week. Roofing marketing is a coordinated system that generates predictable lead flow across all seasons — storm season, replacement season, repair season, and the slow months when most contractors panic.

Here is where it gets interesting: most roofing companies do not have a marketing system. They have a collection of tactics that worked once and never got optimized. A $5,000 Google Ads campaign that generated three leads. A website that looks good but converts at 0.8%. A Google Business Profile that was set up in 2019 and never touched again. The result is what we call "lead whiplash" — weeks of too many leads followed by months of silence.

The U.S. roofing market is valued at $32.66 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $46.67 billion by 2031. That growth is not going to the companies with the best shingles. It is going to the companies with the best marketing systems. Sixty-three and a half percent of market revenue comes from re-roofing and replacement — not new construction. That means your market is homeowners who already have a roof and need to replace it. The question is whether they find you or your competitor first.

Key Takeaway: Roofing marketing is not about finding one magic channel. It is about building a diversified system where no single channel contributes more than 40% of your leads. When storm season ends, your SEO leads keep coming. When SEO takes time to ramp up, your referral network fills the gap. That is the system this guide will help you build.

The 5 Types of Roofing Leads You Need to Understand

Not all roofing leads are equal. A storm damage lead worth $15,000 is not the same as a $400 gutter repair inquiry. Before you spend a dollar on marketing, you need to understand the five lead types and how they flow through your business. We call this The Roofing Revenue Cycle — and it is the framework that separates roofers who scale from roofers who stay stuck.

The 5 Lead Types

Lead Type Average Ticket Close Rate Seasonality Marketing Channel
Storm Damage $12,000–$20,000 25–35% Peak: spring/summer PPC, door-to-door, direct mail
Replacement $8,000–$15,000 20–30% Year-round, peaks fall SEO, referrals, PPC
Repair $400–$2,500 40–60% Year-round SEO, local ads, GBP
New Construction $5,000–$12,000 15–25% Peak: spring/summer Builder relationships, B2B
Commercial $15,000–$100,000+ 10–20% Year-round Networking, LinkedIn, RFPs

Storm damage leads are the highest-value, fastest-closing leads in roofing. Twenty-two percent of all roofing projects originate from storm damage, and 12 million properties were hit by hail in 2024 alone. These homeowners need a roofer immediately — but they also need help navigating insurance claims. The contractor who can guide them through the claims process wins the job.

Replacement leads are the bread and butter of established roofing companies. Forty-four percent of U.S. single-family homes are 30+ years old, and 25% of new homeowners replace the roof within four years of purchase. These leads take longer to close because homeowners comparison-shop, but the ticket size is substantial.

Repair leads close the fastest at 40–60% but have the lowest ticket size. They are valuable for filling gaps between large jobs and for building relationships that lead to future replacements.

New construction and commercial leads require different marketing entirely — builder relationships and B2B networking rather than homeowner-focused advertising.

The Roofing Revenue Cycle

Here is how the cycle works:

  1. Attract: Homeowner becomes aware they need roofing services (storm hits, roof ages, leak appears)
  2. Search: Homeowner searches online, asks neighbors, or sees your ad
  3. Evaluate: Homeowner compares 2–4 contractors based on reviews, website, and responsiveness
  4. Convert: Homeowner books an inspection or estimate
  5. Deliver: You complete the job and deliver exceptional service
  6. Amplify: Satisfied customer leaves a review, refers a neighbor, or becomes a repeat customer

The best roofing companies optimize every stage of this cycle — not just the "Attract" stage. A 10% improvement in close rate is worth more than a 50% increase in lead volume if your follow-up is slow.

Chapter 1: Building Your Roofing Marketing Foundation

Before you run a single ad or write a blog post, you need a foundation. Most roofing companies skip this step and wonder why their marketing feels scattered. Your foundation answers three questions: Who do you serve? What makes you different? And what do you want them to do?

Define Your Ideal Customer

Roofing is not one market. It is at least four: residential replacement, residential repair, storm damage restoration, and commercial. Each requires different messaging, different pricing, and different marketing channels.

Ask yourself:
- Do I want residential or commercial work?
- Do I want high-ticket replacement jobs or quick-turn repair calls?
- Do I chase storms or build year-round revenue?
- What is my geographic sweet spot?

Your answers determine everything that follows. A storm damage specialist in Dallas needs a completely different marketing system than a luxury residential roofer in Scottsdale.

Develop Your Unique Selling Proposition (USP)

Homeowners cannot tell the difference between roofers. To them, you all install shingles. Your USP is what makes you the obvious choice. Here are USPs that actually work in roofing:

Weak USP Strong USP
"Quality workmanship" "We complete 95% of jobs in one day"
"Licensed and insured" "Licensed in 3 states with $2M liability coverage"
"Free estimates" "Free drone inspection + same-day written estimate"
"Family-owned" "Family-owned since 1987 with 4,000+ roofs completed"
"Best prices" "We match any written estimate + 10-year workmanship warranty"

Your USP should be specific, provable, and relevant to your ideal customer. Vague claims like "quality" or "experience" do not differentiate you.

Set Your Service Area Strategy

Many roofers make the mistake of claiming a 100-mile service radius. That sounds impressive, but it destroys your local SEO and operational efficiency. Here is the rule: Only market to areas where you can complete a job start-to-finish within one day. That usually means a 20–30 mile radius.

For each service area, create:
- A dedicated location page on your website
- A separate Google Business Profile listing (if you have a physical location there)
- Neighborhood-specific content addressing local roofing issues

Build Your Marketing Budget Framework

How much should a roofing company spend on marketing? The answer depends on your revenue and growth goals. Here is a framework based on 2025 industry data:

Annual Revenue Marketing Budget (% of revenue) Monthly Spend Primary Channels
$250K–$500K 8–12% $1,700–$5,000 GBP, local SEO, referrals
$500K–$1M 6–10% $2,500–$8,300 SEO + PPC mix, referrals
$1M–$3M 5–8% $4,200–$20,000 Diversified: SEO, PPC, content
$3M+ 4–6% $10,000–$150,000 Full funnel + brand building

The key insight: smaller companies need to spend a higher percentage of revenue because they lack brand recognition and organic traffic. As you grow and your SEO and referral engine mature, your marketing spend as a percentage of revenue can decrease while total lead volume increases.

Action Steps:
1. Choose your primary market segment (residential replacement, storm damage, commercial, or mixed)
2. Write your USP in one sentence
3. Define your exact service area (no more than 30-mile radius)
4. Calculate your marketing budget using the framework above
5. Set a 90-day revenue goal and work backward to required lead volume

Chapter 2: Local SEO for Roofing Companies

Local SEO is the single highest-ROI marketing channel for roofing companies. Period. The Local 3-Pack (the top three map listings on Google) appears in 93% of local searches and captures 44–50% of all clicks. If you are not in the top three map results for "roofing contractor near me," you are invisible to the majority of your market.

Why Local SEO Dominates Roofing

Consider the homeowner behavior: a hailstorm hits. The homeowner pulls out their phone and searches "roofing contractor near me" or "emergency roof repair [city]." They do not scroll past the map. They call one of the first three companies they see. If you are not there, you do not exist in that moment.

The best part? Local SEO leads are free after the initial investment. Unlike PPC where you pay $124–$228 per lead indefinitely, a well-optimized Google Business Profile and website generate leads for years without ongoing per-lead costs.

Google Business Profile Optimization

Your Google Business Profile (GBP) is the single most important digital asset for local SEO. Here is how to optimize it:

Primary Category: Must be "Roofing Contractor." This is used by 94.3% of top-ranking roofers.

Secondary Categories: Add relevant services like Siding Contractor, Gutter Cleaning Service, Storm Damage Restoration, and Window Installation Service.

Photos: Upload at least 10+ high-quality images: before/after shots, crew on job sites, storm damage repairs, and your trucks. Update quarterly. Businesses with complete profiles are 70% more likely to attract location visits.

Weekly Posts: Publish GBP posts every week. Examples: "3 Signs Your Roof Needs Immediate Repair," "How to Spot Hail Damage," or "What to Expect During a Roof Replacement." Google interprets weekly posting as an active, legitimate business.

Q&A Section: Actively monitor and answer questions. This drives engagement signals.

Services & Attributes: List all services clearly. Add attributes like Emergency Service, Free Estimates, Financing Available, and Licensed & Insured.

Service Area: Configure accurately. Setting an unrealistic 100-mile radius where you have no job history can suppress visibility.

Messaging: Enable messaging for instant replies.

Review Generation Systems

Reviews are the #1 prominence signal for local SEO. Here is what the data shows:

  • Roofers with 15+ new reviews per month earn 3x more calls
  • A roofer with 60 reviews at 4.8 stars typically outranks a competitor with 10 reviews at 5.0 stars
  • The first contractor to respond to a lead wins the job approximately 78% of the time
  • Contacting a lead within 1 minute improves conversion rates by up to 391%

Review Generation Tactics:

  1. Automated Text Requests: Send a text within 24 hours of job completion with a direct review link. Customers are 42% more likely to respond immediately after a job is finished.
  2. In-Person Ask: Train crew leaders to ask for reviews on the final walkthrough.
  3. Review Cards: Hand homeowners a physical card with a QR code linking to your GBP.
  4. Follow-Up Sequence: If no review after 3 days, send a gentle reminder. If no review after 7 days, send one final request.

Responding to Reviews: Reply to every review — positive and negative — within 48 hours. For negative reviews, never argue. Acknowledge the concern, offer offline resolution, and stay professional.

Location Page Architecture

Create dedicated landing pages for every city and neighborhood you serve. Do not create one generic "service areas" page. Google rewards specificity.

Each location page should include:
- City/neighborhood name in H1, title tag, and URL
- Local roofing challenges specific to that area (hail frequency, snow load, common materials)
- 2–3 testimonials from customers in that area
- Photos of completed jobs in that neighborhood
- Map embed showing your service area
- Local schema markup

Local Link Building for Roofers

Google's local algorithm weighs prominence heavily. Build local authority through:

  • Chamber of Commerce membership and directory listings
  • Sponsor local sports teams or community events
  • Partner with local real estate agents for referral exchanges
  • Guest posts on local business blogs
  • Get featured in local news (storm damage expertise, community projects)
  • Build citations on 50+ directories (Yelp, Angi, BBB, HomeAdvisor, Thumbtack, Houzz)

NAP Consistency: Your Name, Address, and Phone number must be identical across your website, GBP, and all directories. Even small differences fragment your authority.

Action Steps:
1. Claim and fully optimize your Google Business Profile this week
2. Set up automated text review requests
3. Create location pages for your top 5 service areas
4. Join your local Chamber of Commerce
5. Build citations on the top 20 directories

Chapter 3: Website Design That Converts Roofing Leads

Your website is your 24/7 sales representative. In 2026, it is also your primary credibility tool. Homeowners will visit your website before they call — and if it is slow, confusing, or missing trust signals, they will call your competitor instead.

Roofing Website Conversion Benchmarks

Site Type Conversion Rate
Average roofing website 0.5% – 2%
Healthy/optimized site 3% – 5%
High-performing local pages 5% – 8%
Elite dedicated landing pages 8% – 14.5%

If your site converts below 2%, buying more traffic is the expensive answer. Doubling your conversion rate from 1.2% to 2.4% generates more revenue than any ad campaign expansion.

Must-Have Website Elements for Roofers

1. Dedicated Landing Pages for Each Service

Send traffic to intent-matched landing pages, not your homepage. A roofing contractor improved from 3.56% conversion (general website) to 5.77% (dedicated landing page), dropping cost per lead from $196 to $121 and generating 63 extra leads per month on the exact same budget.

Create separate pages for:
- Roof Replacement
- Roof Repair
- Emergency Roofing
- Storm Damage Restoration
- Gutter Installation
- Commercial Roofing

2. Click-to-Call Buttons (Prominent)

Over 60% of roofing searches happen on mobile. Your phone number should be a large, thumb-sized click-to-call button that is visible without scrolling.

3. Instant Estimate Tool

An online roof quote tool above the fold can dramatically increase conversions. Best practices:
- Use a single, full-width column layout
- Explain how it works to reduce skepticism
- Add urgency: "Get Your Quote in Under 2 Minutes"
- Show a progress indicator

4. Trust Signals

Homeowners are letting strangers onto their property for high-ticket work. Trust signals reduce anxiety:

Trust Signal Implementation
BBB Accreditation Display badge prominently
Manufacturer Certifications GAF, Owens Corning, CertainTeed logos
State License & Insurance License number and insurance details
Years in Business "Serving [City] since [Year]"
Project Count "4,000+ roofs completed"
Real Testimonials Full names, locations, before/after photos
Photo Gallery High-resolution project photos, drone shots

5. Mobile-First Design

Desktop users convert around 4.1%, while mobile users convert around 1.5%. Close that gap by:
- Eliminating multi-field forms on mobile
- Using instant callback options
- Avoiding layouts that require zooming
- Testing mobile variants separately

6. Page Speed

Every 1-second delay in load time reduces conversions by approximately 7%. Target a PageSpeed Insights score of 80+. Compress images, enable caching, and minimize JavaScript.

Storm Damage Landing Pages

Storm damage landing pages are different from standard service pages. They need:

  • Urgent headline: "Free Storm Damage Inspection — We Are in [Neighborhood] Today"
  • Storm-specific proof: Photos of damage from the recent storm
  • Insurance guidance: "We work with all insurance companies"
  • Social proof: "47 homeowners in [Area] have called us this week"
  • Fast CTA: "Call Now for Same-Day Inspection"

These pages should be built before storm season and activated within hours of a hail event.

Action Steps:
1. Audit your current website conversion rate
2. Create dedicated landing pages for your top 3 services
3. Add click-to-call buttons to every page
4. Implement an instant estimate tool
5. Add trust signals above the fold
6. Test mobile speed and fix issues

Chapter 4: Storm Damage and Emergency Lead Generation

Storm damage leads are the highest-value, fastest-closing leads in roofing. The average storm damage ticket is $12,000–$20,000, and homeowners need immediate help. But here is the catch: the window to capture these leads is 24–48 hours after a storm. After that, your competitors have already knocked on their doors.

The Storm Damage Lead Opportunity

Twenty-two percent of all roofing projects originate from storm damage. In 2024, 12 million properties were hit by hail. Insurance carriers are shortening acceptable roof ages to 15–20 years, which means more claims and more replacement opportunities. The contractors who master storm marketing can add $500,000 to $2 million in annual revenue from storm seasons alone.

The 24–48 Hour Golden Window

Homeowners decide who gets their roof within 24–48 hours of a hail event. Contractors who flip on pre-built campaigns within minutes — not days — dominate the market. The 5-minute rule applies: roofers who respond to inquiries within 5 minutes convert at 2–3x the rate of those who take an hour.

Pre-Storm Preparation Checklist:

  • [ ] Build storm-specific landing pages for each service area
  • [ ] Pre-write Google Ads campaigns for emergency roofing keywords
  • [ ] Pre-design direct mail postcards for storm-affected zip codes
  • [ ] Set up geo-targeted Facebook ads ready to activate
  • [ ] Train canvassing crews on hail identification and proper approach
  • [ ] Establish relationships with insurance adjusters before storm season
  • [ ] Create a "storm response" email template for your list

Precision Targeting: Find the Hail Before Your Competitors

Do not blanket an entire metro. Use forensic-grade storm data to target block-by-block:

Tool What It Does
HailTrace Real-time zip-code and address-level hail swath data
Interactive Hail Maps Street-level storm tracking
NOAA / NSSL Official radar overlays
GAF WeatherHub Search storm history by city or zip
Permit Tracking Identify where competitors are already pulling permits

Skip yellow zones. Hit red zones (1-inch+ hail). Deploy reps with hail swath maps, not random streets.

The Insurance Adjuster Angle

Most homeowners have never filed a roof claim and are intimidated by the process. Your marketing should position you as the expert guide, not just the roofer.

The Winning Offer: "Free Roof Inspection + Adjuster Meeting Support"

This converts because you are solving the homeowner's fear of the unknown, not just selling a roof.

Key Messaging Points:
- Attend the Adjuster Meeting: Promise to meet the insurance adjuster on-site to ensure damage is not missed
- Documentation & Supplements: Emphasize that you handle technical documentation and supplement negotiations
- Know the Lingo: Reference RCV (Replacement Cost Value) vs. ACV (Actual Cash Value)
- Zero Out-of-Pocket: Where legal, frame it as the homeowner paying only their deductible

Warning: Zero-deductible advertising is banned in Texas, Colorado, and Oklahoma. Always verify state advertising laws.

Storm Marketing Channel Stack

Channel Role Timeline
Google LSAs Capture ready-to-call homeowners Activate immediately
Geo-Targeted PPC Target 5–15 mile radius around hardest-hit blocks Activate within 2 hours
Facebook/Meta Ads Before/after creative with urgent CTAs Activate within 4 hours
Door-to-Door Deploy with hail swath maps Start within 24 hours
Direct Mail Postcards to affected zip codes Mail within 72 hours
Local SEO/GBP Storm damage pages capture search surge Pre-built, auto-activate

Action Steps:
1. Build storm landing pages for your top 5 service areas before storm season
2. Sign up for HailTrace or similar storm tracking
3. Pre-write ad campaigns for emergency keywords
4. Establish relationships with 3–5 insurance adjusters
5. Create a storm response protocol with specific timelines

Chapter 5: Paid Advertising for Roofers

Paid advertising is the fastest way to generate roofing leads — and the fastest way to burn money if you do it wrong. Roofing consistently ranks as the most expensive home services vertical to market. Google Ads costs for roofing keywords jumped 19% year-over-year. But done correctly, paid ads deliver immediate, measurable leads.

Cost Per Lead by Channel (2025–2026 Data)

Channel Avg. Cost Per Lead Lead Quality Best For
Google Ads (Non-Branded) $124–$228 High intent Replacement, emergency
Google Ads (Branded) ~$44 Very high intent Protecting your brand
Google LSAs $50–$150 Medium-High Local lead capture
Facebook/Instagram Ads $30–$100 Medium Brand awareness, storms
Lead Aggregators (Angi, etc.) $40–$150 Low (shared) Filling gaps only
Direct Mail $90–$245 Medium Storm targeting

The gap between the best and worst-performing Google Ads accounts is nearly 10x: $69/lead vs. $674/lead. The difference is not budget. It is targeting, landing pages, and follow-up speed.

Google Ads for Roofing

Keyword Strategy:

Bid on high-intent, long-tail keywords rather than broad terms:

Avoid Target Instead
"roofing" "roof replacement [city]"
"roofer" "emergency roof repair near me"
"roof" "hail damage roof inspection [city]"
"roofing company" "best roofing contractor [neighborhood]"

Ad Copy Best Practices:

  • Include numbers: "15+ Years in [City]" or "Same-Day Inspections"
  • Emphasize urgency: "Storm Damage? Call Now — We Are in [Area] Today"
  • Use ad extensions: call extensions, location extensions, sitelinks
  • A/B test continuously: one roofing campaign increased conversions by 18% by emphasizing "same-day inspection" in headlines

Landing Page Alignment:

Your landing page headline must match your ad copy exactly. If someone searches "emergency roof leak repair," they should land on an emergency page — not a generic services page.

Google Local Services Ads (LSAs)

LSAs appear at the very top of search results with a "Google Guaranteed" badge. You pay per lead (call or message), not per click.

Pros:
- Top-of-page placement
- Google Guaranteed badge builds trust
- Pay-per-lead model

Cons:
- 67% of contractors say LSA lead quality declined in 2025
- Google removed junk-lead credits
- Less control over targeting than traditional PPC

Best practice: Use LSAs as part of a diversified paid strategy, not your only channel.

Facebook and Instagram Ads

Social ads work best for:
- Storm damage awareness (before homeowners know they need a roofer)
- Brand building in your service area
- Retargeting website visitors
- Video testimonials and before/after content

Targeting:
- Homeowners aged 35–65 in your service area
- Interest: home improvement, real estate, insurance
- Behavior: recent home purchase, home value $200K+
- AI-powered targeting can now micro-target homeowners with aging roofs (15+ years)

Lead Aggregator Comparison

Service Cost Lead Type Close Rate
HomeAdvisor $50–$150 Shared (3–5 contractors) 10–15%
Angi $40–$120 Shared 10–15%
Thumbtack $30–$80 Shared or exclusive 15–20%

Shared leads are sold to multiple contractors simultaneously. Homeowners get bombarded by competitors and default to the lowest price. Exclusive leads from your own website or ads close at 30–50%.

Rule: Lead aggregators should be a supplement, not your primary channel. Budget no more than 15% of your paid spend on shared leads.

Budget Allocation by Revenue Level

Monthly Revenue Monthly Ad Budget Recommended Split
$20K–$40K $1,500–$3,000 70% Google Ads, 30% Facebook
$40K–$80K $3,000–$6,000 60% Google Ads, 30% Facebook, 10% LSAs
$80K–$150K $6,000–$12,000 50% Google Ads, 25% Facebook, 15% LSAs, 10% retargeting
$150K+ $12,000+ Full funnel with brand campaigns

Action Steps:
1. Audit your current cost per lead by channel
2. Reallocate budget from lowest-performing channels
3. Build dedicated landing pages for every ad group
4. Set up call tracking to measure true ROI
5. Implement automated follow-up for all paid leads

Chapter 6: Referral and Partnership Marketing

Referral leads are the highest-quality, lowest-cost leads in roofing. They close at 30–50%+, have the highest lifetime value, and cost only $10–$25 in incentive cost. Yet most roofing companies treat referrals as an afterthought instead of a system.

Insurance Agent Partnerships

Insurance agents are your highest-value partners. When a homeowner files a claim, the agent often recommends a roofer. Being that recommended roofer is worth hundreds of thousands in annual revenue.

How to Build Insurance Agent Relationships:

  1. Identify agents who write homeowner policies in your service area
  2. Offer value first: Provide free roof inspections for their clients, educational materials on roofing claims, or CE courses on roof damage assessment
  3. Make it easy: Give agents a one-page "preferred contractor" sheet they can hand to clients
  4. Stay top-of-mind: Quarterly check-ins, holiday gifts, and prompt service on their referrals
  5. Track and reward: Know which agents send you the most business and reward them accordingly

Real Estate Agent Relationships

Real estate agents need roofers for:
- Pre-listing inspections
- Repair credits during negotiations
- Replacement before closing

Partner with top-producing agents in your market. Offer:
- 24-hour inspection turnaround
- Written reports with photos
- Direct communication with the agent (not just the homeowner)

Property Management Companies

Commercial and multi-family property managers need ongoing roofing maintenance and replacement. These relationships produce recurring revenue, not one-off jobs.

Approach:
- Offer annual roof inspection programs
- Provide bulk pricing for portfolio work
- Create a dedicated portal for property managers to request service

Customer Referral Programs

Your past customers are a goldmine. One Florida roofing company boosted referrals by 40% using gamified referral programs with leaderboards and monthly prizes.

Effective Referral Program Structure:

Tier Reward Condition
Standard $100–$250 gift card For each referred job booked
VIP $500 + entry into quarterly drawing For 3+ referrals in a year
Advocate Free annual inspection + priority scheduling For 5+ lifetime refer
rals

Best Practices:
- Ask for referrals at the final walkthrough (not months later)
- Make it easy: give customers referral cards with QR codes
- Follow up: send a "thank you" gift when referrals convert
- Stay visible: email past customers seasonally (not just when you want something)

Contractor Referral Networks

Build relationships with:
- HVAC contractors (roof and HVAC often fail together)
- Siding and gutter companies
- General contractors
- Painters and remodelers

Create a formal referral exchange: you send them leads, they send you leads.

Action Steps:
1. List your top 10 potential referral partners
2. Reach out to 3 this week with a value-first offer
3. Create a referral program with clear rewards
4. Add referral requests to your job completion process
5. Track referral source ROI monthly

Chapter 7: Content Marketing for Roofing Companies

Content marketing builds trust before the homeowner ever calls you. In roofing — where the average ticket is $8,000–$15,000 and homeowners fear being ripped off — trust is everything. Content that educates and demonstrates expertise positions you as the authority homeowners choose.

Blog Topics That Generate Roofing Leads

Topic Search Intent Funnel Stage
"How much does a roof replacement cost in [City]?" Informational MOFU
"How to tell if your roof has hail damage" Informational TOFU
"How long does a roof last?" Informational TOFU
"What to expect during a roof replacement" Informational MOFU
"Best roofing materials for [Climate]" Commercial MOFU
"How to file a roof insurance claim" Informational MOFU
"Roofing contractor vs. storm chaser: how to tell" Commercial MOFU

Content strategy: Extract 5–10 pieces of content from a single roofing project. One hail damage repair can produce:
- Before/after photo gallery
- "How to identify hail damage" blog post
- Video walkthrough of the inspection
- Customer testimonial
- "What happens during a roof replacement" explainer

This reduces content production costs by 30–40% while maintaining authenticity.

Video Content Strategies

Video is the highest-engagement content format for roofers:

  • Video testimonials: 15–30 second clips outperform text reviews by 300% in engagement
  • Educational videos: 2–3 minute clips answering common questions
  • Storm damage walkthroughs: Film inspections in storm-hit neighborhoods
  • Behind-the-scenes: Show your crew at work, safety protocols, and quality checks
  • Before/after transformations: Drone footage showing the full scope of work

Post videos on YouTube, Instagram Reels, TikTok, and Facebook. Repurpose the same content across all platforms.

Social Media for Roofers

Nextdoor is the most underrated platform for roofers. Active Nextdoor accounts generate 2–3 hyperlocal leads per week at $0 cost. Post about:
- Local projects (with homeowner permission)
- Storm damage warnings
- Educational tips
- Community involvement

Facebook and Instagram:
- Post 3–5 times per week
- Mix of educational, proof, and personal content
- Respond to every comment within 2 hours
- Use Stories for behind-the-scenes content

Email Marketing

Your past customers and website visitors are your warmest audience. Use email to:
- Send seasonal reminders (pre-storm inspections, post-winter checks)
- Follow up on unconverted estimates
- Request reviews
- Announce referral programs
- Share new content

Segment your list:
- Past customers (referral focus)
- Unconverted estimates (re-engagement)
- Website visitors who did not contact (nurture)
- Commercial contacts (B2B messaging)

Educational Content

Homeowners research roofing decisions extensively. Be the source they find:

  • Roof lifespan by material
  • Cost guides by roof size and material
  • Insurance claim guides
  • Seasonal maintenance checklists
  • Material comparison guides

Action Steps:
1. Create a content calendar with 12 blog topics
2. Film one video testimonial per month
3. Post on Nextdoor weekly
4. Set up automated email sequences for past customers
5. Build a resource library on your website

The Content Multiplication Strategy

Most roofing companies create one piece of content and move on. Top performers extract 10+ pieces from every project:

One roof replacement becomes:
1. Before/after photo gallery (website)
2. Time-lapse video (YouTube, Instagram Reels, TikTok)
3. "How to choose roofing materials" blog post
4. Customer video testimonial
5. Drone footage for portfolio
6. Social media post series (5–7 posts)
7. Email case study for nurture sequence
8. Sales presentation slide
9. Google Business Profile photo update
10. Nextdoor neighborhood post

This approach reduces content production costs by 30–40% while maintaining authenticity. Every job is a content opportunity.

Platform Frequency Content Mix

Roofers who post only promotional content get ignored. Roofers who educate and entertain build audiences that convert when they are ready.

Chapter 8: Tracking, Measurement, and ROI

You cannot improve what you do not measure. Most roofing companies track only one metric: how many leads came in this month. That is like driving with only a speedometer — you know how fast you are going, but not if you are heading in the right direction.

KPIs Every Roofing Company Should Track

Metric Why It Matters Target
Cost Per Lead (CPL) Efficiency of each channel Varies by channel (see Chapter 5)
Cost Per Sale True marketing ROI Track monthly
Lead Volume by Source Which channels deliver Monthly review
Conversion Rate (Lead to Sale) Sales effectiveness 15–30%
Average Ticket Size Revenue per job Track by lead source
Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) Total cost to get one customer Under 15% of ticket
Lifetime Value (LTV) Long-term customer worth 2–3x first ticket
Review Velocity Local SEO health 10–15/month
Website Conversion Rate Site effectiveness 3–5%
Speed-to-Lead Response time Under 5 minutes

Call Tracking Setup

Many roofing leads call rather than fill out forms. Without call tracking, you do not know which marketing channel generated the call.

Implement:
- Unique phone numbers for each channel (Google Ads, Facebook, organic, direct mail)
- Call recording for quality assurance
- Missed call alerts with automatic callback
- Integration with your CRM

Lead Source Attribution

Use a simple attribution model:

First Touch Last Touch Weighting
Where the lead first found you What made them contact you 40% first touch, 60% last touch

Example: A homeowner first sees your Google Ad (first touch) but calls two weeks later after seeing your truck (last touch). Both channels contributed.

ROI Calculation Framework

Basic ROI Formula:

ROI = (Revenue from Marketing - Marketing Cost) / Marketing Cost × 100

Example:
- Monthly marketing spend: $5,000
- Leads generated: 50
- Close rate: 20% (10 sales)
- Average ticket: $10,000
- Revenue: $100,000
- ROI: ($100,000 - $5,000) / $5,000 = 1,900%

Advanced: Cost Per Sale by Channel

Channel CPL Close Rate Cost Per Sale
Google Ads $150 20% $750
SEO $0* 25% $0*
Referrals $25 40% $63
Facebook $75 15% $500

*SEO has upfront investment but no per-lead cost after ranking.

Action Steps:
1. Set up call tracking with unique numbers per channel
2. Create a simple dashboard tracking the 10 KPIs above
3. Review marketing ROI monthly
4. Reallocate budget from lowest-performing channels
5. Set up automated reporting

Chapter 9: The 12 Roofing Marketing Mistakes Costing You $50K+ (And How to Fix Them)

After auditing hundreds of roofing companies' marketing, we see the same mistakes repeatedly. These are not small errors — they cost companies tens of thousands in lost revenue every year.

Mistake 1: Relying on a Single Lead Source

The roofers who struggle most are those who get 80% of their leads from one channel — usually storm chasing or HomeAdvisor. When that channel dries up, so does their revenue.

The fix: Build a diversified lead system. No single channel should contribute more than 40% of your leads. Aim for: 30% SEO/local, 25% paid ads, 25% referrals, 10% content/social, 10% other.

Mistake 2: Sending Paid Traffic to Your Homepage

Your homepage is not a landing page. It is a navigation tool. When someone clicks a Google Ad for "emergency roof repair" and lands on your homepage, they have to figure out where to go next. Most will not bother.

The fix: Build dedicated landing pages for every service and every campaign. Match the headline to the ad copy exactly. Include one clear CTA. Remove navigation menus if possible.

Mistake 3: Ignoring Mobile Experience

Sixty-one percent of roofing searches happen on mobile. Yet most roofing websites are designed on desktop and barely function on phones. Mobile users convert at 1.5% vs. 4.1% on desktop.

The fix: Design mobile-first. Test every page on an actual phone. Make phone numbers thumb-sized click-to-call buttons. Eliminate multi-field forms. Use instant callback options.

Mistake 4: Slow Follow-Up

The first contractor to respond wins the job approximately 78% of the time. Delaying follow-up by 24 hours drops conversion rates by 40%. Yet most roofing companies let leads sit for hours.

The fix: Implement automated text responses within 60 seconds of any inquiry. Use CRM automation to trigger follow-up texts at 1 hour, 24 hours, and 72 hours. Set up call routing so no call goes to voicemail.

Mistake 5: No Review Generation System

Roofers with 15+ new reviews per month earn 3x more calls. Yet most companies treat reviews as something that happens organically. They do not.

The fix: Set up automated text review requests that send within 24 hours of job completion. Include a direct link to your Google Business Profile. Train crew leaders to ask in person. Follow up once if no response.

Mistake 6: Buying Shared Leads Exclusively

HomeAdvisor, Angi, and Thumbtack sell the same lead to 3–5 contractors simultaneously. Homeowners get bombarded with calls and default to the lowest price. Close rates on shared leads are 10–15% vs. 30–50% for exclusive leads.

The fix: Use lead aggregators as a supplement only — no more than 15% of your paid budget. Invest in channels that generate exclusive leads: your own website, Google Ads, and referrals.

Mistake 7: No Seasonal Strategy

Most roofers market heavily during storm season and go silent the rest of the year. Then they panic when leads dry up in winter.

The fix: Build a 12-month marketing calendar (see below). Market differently in each season. Use slow months for content creation, website improvements, and referral program pushes.

Mistake 8: Generic Messaging

"Quality workmanship since 1995" tells homeowners nothing. Every roofer says they do quality work. Vague claims do not differentiate you.

The fix: Be specific. "We complete 95% of jobs in one day." "Same-day written estimates." "Free drone inspection included." Specificity builds trust.

Mistake 9: No Call Tracking

If you do not track which marketing channel generated each call, you are flying blind. You cannot optimize what you do not measure.

The fix: Implement call tracking with unique numbers for each channel: Google Ads, Facebook, organic search, direct mail, and referrals. Review monthly and reallocate budget to highest-performing channels.

Mistake 10: Neglecting Past Customers

Your past customers are your warmest audience. They already trust you. Yet most roofers never email, call, or mail them again after the job is done.

The fix: Email past customers seasonally with maintenance tips, referral program reminders, and inspection offers. A simple "How is your roof holding up?" email can generate repair calls and referrals.

Mistake 11: Using Stock Photos

Stock photos of generic houses tell homeowners you are hiding something. Authenticity matters in roofing.

The fix: Document every job. Take before/after photos. Film short video walkthroughs. Use real crew photos. Even imperfect authentic photos build more trust than polished stock images.

Mistake 12: No Website Conversion Optimization

The average roofing website converts at 0.5–2%. That means 98% of visitors leave without contacting you. Optimized sites reach 8–14.5%.

The fix: Add instant estimate tools, click-to-call buttons, trust signals, and before/after galleries. A/B test headlines and CTAs. Even a 1% improvement in conversion rate can double your leads without spending more on ads.

Your 12-Month Roofing Marketing Calendar

Roofing is seasonal. Your marketing should be too. Here is a month-by-month calendar that accounts for the industry's natural rhythms.

Weather-Triggered Marketing

Smart roofers tie marketing to weather events:

  • 48 hours before a storm: Send email/SMS to past customers with preparation tips
  • Within 6 hours after hail: Activate geo-targeted PPC and social ads
  • 24–48 hours after: Deploy door-to-door canvassers with hail maps
  • 72 hours after: Mail postcards to affected neighborhoods
  • 1 week after: Publish "What to do after hail damage" blog post
  • 2 weeks after: Retarget website visitors with social ads

This weather-triggered approach ensures you are first to market when demand spikes.

Slow Season Marketing (November–February)

Most roofers go quiet in winter. That is a mistake. Slow season is when you:

  1. Build systems: Implement automation, CRM, and tracking
  2. Create content: Film videos, write blog posts, design infographics
  3. Strengthen partnerships: Meet with insurance agents, realtors, and property managers
  4. Train your team: Sales training, customer service, and technical skills
  5. Plan for storm season: Build landing pages, write ad copy, prepare direct mail
  6. Reach past customers: Offer winter inspections and maintenance programs

The roofers who market consistently in slow season dominate when peak season arrives because their systems are already running.

Roofing Marketing Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best way to market a roofing company?

The best approach is a diversified system combining local SEO, paid advertising, and referral marketing. Local SEO (especially your Google Business Profile) delivers the highest long-term ROI. Paid ads generate immediate leads. Referrals provide the highest-quality, lowest-cost leads. No single channel should contribute more than 40% of your leads.

How much should a roofing company spend on marketing?

Roofing companies should spend 5–12% of revenue on marketing, depending on size. Companies under $500K should spend 8–12%. Companies over $3M can spend 4–6% because their brand recognition and organic traffic reduce acquisition costs. The key metric is not spend — it is cost per sale and overall ROI.

How do roofers get leads?

Roofers get leads through six primary channels: local SEO and Google Business Profile (highest ROI long-term), paid advertising like Google Ads and Facebook (fastest results), referral networks and partnerships (highest close rates), storm damage marketing (highest ticket size), content marketing (builds trust over time), and lead aggregators like HomeAdvisor (lowest quality but fills gaps).

What is the average cost per lead for roofing?

Cost per lead varies dramatically by channel. Google Ads averages $124–$228 per lead. Google Local Services Ads range from $50–$150. Facebook and Instagram ads average $30–$100. Lead aggregators like Angi and HomeAdvisor charge $40–$150 for shared leads. Referrals cost $10–$25 in incentive costs. SEO leads have no per-lead cost after the initial investment.

How do I get storm damage leads?

Storm damage leads require speed and precision. Use hail tracking tools like HailTrace to identify affected neighborhoods within hours of a storm. Activate pre-built PPC campaigns, deploy door-to-door canvassers with hail swath maps, and mail postcards to affected zip codes within 72 hours. The golden window is 24–48 hours after the storm.

Should roofers use PPC or SEO?

Use both. SEO is a long-term investment that delivers free leads once you rank, but it takes 3–6 months to see results. PPC delivers immediate leads but requires ongoing budget. The ideal strategy: use PPC for immediate cash flow and storm season, while building SEO for sustainable, low-cost lead generation year-round.

How important are reviews for roofing companies?

Reviews are critical. Thirty-five percent of homeowners rely on online reviews during contractor selection. Roofers with 15+ new reviews per month earn 3x more calls. Google considers review volume, velocity, and response rate as primary ranking factors for local SEO. Every roofing company should have an automated review request system.

What should a roofing company website include?

A roofing website needs: dedicated landing pages for each service, prominent click-to-call buttons, trust signals (licenses, insurance, certifications), before/after photo galleries, real customer testimonials, an instant estimate tool, and mobile-optimized design. The average roofing website converts at 0.5–2%, but optimized sites reach 8–14.5%.

How can roofers get more commercial leads?

Commercial roofing requires B2B relationship building, not homeowner advertising. Build relationships with property management companies, general contractors, and facility managers. Offer annual maintenance programs. Join commercial real estate associations. Use LinkedIn for targeted outreach. Commercial leads have longer sales cycles but much higher ticket sizes ($15,000–$100,000+).

What marketing works best for roofers?

The highest-ROI marketing for roofers is local SEO combined with Google Business Profile optimization, followed by referral marketing. For immediate leads, Google Ads targeting high-intent keywords performs best. Storm damage marketing delivers the highest-value leads but requires rapid response. The key is diversification — no single channel should dominate.

How fast should roofers respond to leads?

Speed is critical. Contacting a lead within 1 minute improves conversion rates by up to 391%. The first contractor to respond wins the job approximately 78% of the time. Seventy percent of contractors now reply within 4 hours, but the top performers use automated systems to respond in under 5 minutes.

Do financing options help roofing sales?

Yes. Offering 0% down or multiple payment plans can improve lead conversion by up to 42%. Many homeowners delay roof replacement because they cannot afford the upfront cost. Financing removes that barrier. Promote financing prominently on your website and in your marketing materials.

How do I track ROI on roofing marketing?

Track cost per lead by channel, lead-to-sale conversion rate, average ticket size by source, and overall customer acquisition cost. Use call tracking with unique numbers per channel. Calculate ROI monthly using the formula: (Revenue from Marketing - Marketing Cost) / Marketing Cost × 100. The best metric is cost per sale, not cost per lead.

What is the difference between exclusive and shared leads?

Exclusive leads come directly to you through your own website, ads, or referrals. They close at 30–50%. Shared leads from aggregators like HomeAdvisor are sold to 3–5 contractors simultaneously. They close below 10–15% because homeowners get bombarded by competitors and default to the lowest price. Always prioritize exclusive lead channels.

How long does SEO take for roofing companies?

Most roofing companies see initial ranking movement within 30–60 days, with significant Map Pack improvements in 60–90 days. Competitive top-3 positions usually require 3–6 months of sustained effort. SEO is a long-term investment — the leads it generates after month 6 cost essentially nothing.

What is the Roofing Revenue Cycle?

The Roofing Revenue Cycle is a six-stage framework that describes how roofing leads flow through your business: Attract (homeowner becomes aware they need roofing), Search (they look for contractors), Evaluate (they compare options), Convert (they book an inspection), Deliver (you complete the job), and Amplify (satisfied customers refer others). The best roofing companies optimize every stage — not just lead generation.

How do I choose between residential and commercial roofing marketing?

Residential marketing focuses on homeowner education, local SEO, storm damage, and referral programs. Commercial marketing requires B2B relationship building, LinkedIn outreach, RFP responses, and networking with property managers and general contractors. Most companies under $2M should focus on residential first, then add commercial as a secondary market.

What makes a roofing website convert?

High-converting roofing websites have five elements: dedicated landing pages for each service, prominent click-to-call buttons, strong trust signals (licenses, certifications, testimonials), before/after photo galleries, and mobile-first design. The average roofing website converts at 0.5–2%, but optimized sites reach 8–14.5%.

Should I hire a marketing agency or do it in-house?

Companies under $1M often get better results with in-house execution guided by a consultant, because agencies charge minimum retainers ($2,000–$5,000/month) that consume too much of a small budget. Companies over $2M benefit from agency expertise in PPC management, SEO, and content at scale. The hybrid approach — in-house for referrals and local SEO, agency for PPC and technical SEO — often works best.

How do I compete with storm chasers?

Storm chasers have one advantage: speed. You compete by being faster and more trustworthy. Build pre-storm landing pages and ad campaigns ready to activate. Establish insurance adjuster relationships before storm season. Emphasize your local roots, licensing, and warranty. Position yourself as the permanent local roofer who will be there for warranty claims — unlike storm chasers who leave town.

What is the best roofing CRM?

The best CRM is the one your team actually uses. Popular options for roofers include AccuLynx, JobNimbus, Roofr, and Contractor Foreman. Key features to look for: automated text/email follow-up, pipeline tracking, document management, and integration with your accounting software. A simple CRM used consistently beats a complex CRM abandoned after two weeks.

Marketing is not about finding a magic tactic. It is about building systems that compound. The roofing companies dominating their markets in 2026 are not luckier than you. They are more systematic. Start building your system today.
